questions.q: “Paradise lies under the feet of the mother.” To whom does the article say this saying is really addressed, and with what meaning?
options: To the child – obedience alone earns Paradise
Not quite. The article says: To the mother – she carries the great responsibility of shaping her child into a good human being.
To teachers – they replace the mother
Not quite. The article says: To the mother – she carries the great responsibility of shaping her child into a good human being.
To the mother – she carries the great responsibility of shaping her child into a good human being
Yes. Its usual reading, as only a demand on the child, misses this.
To the father – he must provide for the mother
Not quite. The article says: To the mother – she carries the great responsibility of shaping her child into a good human being.
questions.rationale: “This Hadith actually addresses a mother… it is in the hands of the mother to create a passion for Paradise in a human being.”

questions.q: Why does the article stress the first ten years of a child’s life?
options: Children learn nothing after ten
Not quite. The article says: It is the formative period – the personality shaped then remains through later life.
It is when children are easiest to feed
Not quite. The article says: It is the formative period – the personality shaped then remains through later life.
It is the formative period – the personality shaped then remains through later life
Right. And children imitate their mothers most.
Schooling ends at ten
Not quite. The article says: It is the formative period – the personality shaped then remains through later life.
questions.rationale: “In this formative period, the personality that is formed within someone remains throughout the later age.”

questions.q: What did Maulana learn from finding that a summer fast he had dreaded passed easily?
options: Fasting should be avoided by the weak
Not quite. The article says: A task begun with trust in God is made easy by His help.
Fear is always justified
Not quite. The article says: A task begun with trust in God is made easy by His help.
A task begun with trust in God is made easy by His help
Yes. Fasting is a lesson in morale.
Summer fasts are shorter than winter ones
Not quite. The article says: A task begun with trust in God is made easy by His help.
questions.rationale: “No matter how difficult a task in God’s way may seem, if you start this work on God’s trust, God’s help will be with you.”

questions.article: Man in the World of God
questions.q: For what purpose, according to the article, has man been given the means to see the vastness of the universe?
options: So that he may feel important
Not quite. The article says: So that he may wonder at the greatness of its Creator and come to know Him.
So that he may travel to other galaxies
Not quite. The article says: So that he may wonder at the greatness of its Creator and come to know Him.
So that he may wonder at the greatness of its Creator and come to know Him
Well read. Not only to answer questions about creation.
So that he may map the stars for trade
Not quite. The article says: So that he may wonder at the greatness of its Creator and come to know Him.
questions.rationale: “This is so that man may see the universe in all its greatness, and then wonder at the greatness of the One who created it.”

questions.q: A student who had failed three times saw a stone worn hollow by clay pots at a well. What did he conclude?
options: He should give up his studies
Not quite. The article says: Constant effort lets even the weak wear down the strong – so he too could succeed by persevering.
Clay is harder than stone
Not quite. The article says: Constant effort lets even the weak wear down the strong – so he too could succeed by persevering.
Stones at wells should be replaced
Not quite. The article says: Constant effort lets even the weak wear down the strong – so he too could succeed by persevering.
Constant effort lets even the weak wear down the strong – so he too could succeed by persevering
Correct. He went on to earn a doctorate.
questions.rationale: “The strong element had given way to the weak just through constant action. ‘Then why should I not succeed in my examinations if I too persevere?’”

questions.q: How does the article describe the second of its three types – the occasional wrongdoer?
options: He ranks highest of all
Not quite. The article says: He can be forgiven if he is a true believer, makes amends by good deeds and turns to God in penitence.
He need do nothing at all
Not quite. The article says: He can be forgiven if he is a true believer, makes amends by good deeds and turns to God in penitence.
He is beyond all forgiveness
Not quite. The article says: He can be forgiven if he is a true believer, makes amends by good deeds and turns to God in penitence.
He can be forgiven if he is a true believer, makes amends by good deeds and turns to God in penitence
Yes. He is not obstinate in wrong.
questions.rationale: “He too can be forgiven by God and share His blessings, provided he is a true believer… All he has to do then is turn to God in penitence.”

questions.q: An inventor’s patent lasts a limited time. Why does the article say the Creator’s right over creation is eternal?
options: No one has challenged it
Not quite. The article says: A human invention draws on nature and other people; the Creator made His creation alone, with no partner.
A human invention draws on nature and other people; the Creator made His creation alone, with no partner
Right. And He sustains it every moment.
Human laws do not apply in nature
Not quite. The article says: A human invention draws on nature and other people; the Creator made His creation alone, with no partner.
Creation is older than any patent
Not quite. The article says: A human invention draws on nature and other people; the Creator made His creation alone, with no partner.
questions.rationale: “Unlike man’s invention, there is no contribution by anyone in the Creator’s invention… The Creator’s monopoly over creation is eternal.”

questions.q: What does the article call the “royalty” that man owes to God?
options: Worship of God and willing submission to Him
Yes. Given by free choice.
Nothing at all
Not quite. The article says: Worship of God and willing submission to Him.
A fee for natural resources
Not quite. The article says: Worship of God and willing submission to Him.
A share of his income to the state
Not quite. The article says: Worship of God and willing submission to Him.
questions.rationale: “Royalty that is due to God is worship of God and total submission to Him.”

questions.q: Besides increasing our own knowledge, what advantage does the article see in listening first?
options: We appear wiser than we are
Not quite. The article says: We learn the other person’s view, and so can speak to it persuasively and with consideration.
We learn the other person’s view, and so can speak to it persuasively and with consideration
Exactly. “I have often regretted my speech, never my silence.”
The other person tires and stops
Not quite. The article says: We learn the other person’s view, and so can speak to it persuasively and with consideration.
We need not speak at all
Not quite. The article says: We learn the other person’s view, and so can speak to it persuasively and with consideration.
questions.rationale: “We know in advance what misapprehensions we have to sweep aside, what illusions we have to dispel and what emotional barriers we have to break down.”

questions.q: The Prophet told a man not to waste water “even if you are on the banks of a flowing river.” What attitude does the article say leads to such care?
options: Gratitude – one who truly values water as God’s gift asks, “If I cannot create water, how can I waste it?”
Well reasoned. Spirituality is this thankfulness.
Dislike of water
Not quite. The article says: Gratitude – one who truly values water as God’s gift asks, “If I cannot create water, how can I waste it?”.
A wish to save money
Not quite. The article says: Gratitude – one who truly values water as God’s gift asks, “If I cannot create water, how can I waste it?”.
Fear of a fine
Not quite. The article says: Gratitude – one who truly values water as God’s gift asks, “If I cannot create water, how can I waste it?”.
questions.rationale: “A person who is truly grateful to God for the blessings of water will ask himself: ‘If I cannot create water, how can I waste it?’”
